ratings.plot: The great Frank Zappa's outrageous psychedelic precursor to today's music videos features "The Mothers of Invention" wreaking havoc in a typical American town. Ringo Starr narrates.

verdict.reason: A genuine curiosity—Zappa's only narrative film feature with Ringo as narrator and the Mothers trashing a small town—but the 98 minutes feel scattered and the joke wears thin fast. The Alamo Drafthouse screening rewards adventurous viewers who want to experience Zappa's chaos on a big screen, but this is a film that works better as artifact than as entertainment.

ratings.plot: Several women enter a science fiction author's life over the course of a few years, after the author has lost the woman he considers his one true love.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's most visually ambitious film demands a theater screen and Metrograph's DCP restoration lets the neon-soaked production design breathe. The 129-minute runtime tests patience, but the payoff is a rare work of sci-fi romance that uses visual style as narrative itself.

ratings.plot: Two roommates/physical therapists, one a vain woman and the other an awkward teenager, share an increasingly bizarre relationship.

verdict.reason: Altman's most cryptic and visually assured film demands the big screen—a dreamlike mystery that only deepens on repeat viewings. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the pastel production design and spatial compositions that make the psychic entanglement between these women feel inevitable rather than explained.

The film has genuine emotional weight but plays better as a home viewing than as a theatrical outing. IFC Center is the right venue, but the intimate scale and modest scope don't demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: Henry Graham lives the life of a playboy. When his lawyer tells him that his lifestyle has consumed all his funds, Henry must avoid climbing down the social ladder. He plans to marry wealthy scientist Henrietta Lowell - and kill her.

verdict.reason: Worth seeing for May's brilliant directorial debut, which she also wrote and starred in with perfect misanthropic timing. Her chemistry with Walter Matthau creates one of the sharpest dark comedies of the 1970s.

ratings.plot: The Addams Family try to rescue their beloved Uncle Fester from his gold-digging new love, a black widow named Debbie.

verdict.reason: A sequel sharper and funnier than the original, worth catching on the big screen for Sonnenfeld's visual invention and the entire cast firing at full strength. Joan Cusack's performance as Debbie Jellinsky alone justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Ridley Scott making a post-apocalyptic movie is all you need to say to get us interested. THE DOG STARS swaps zombie hordes and wasteland spectacle for something quieter and more haunting: a survival story about the people who keep searching for hope after the world has already ended. Jacob Elordi leads an incredible ensemble that includes Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley, Allison Janney, Benedict Wong, and a grizzled-looking Guy Pearce. And yes, there is a dog in THE DOG STARS. His name is Jasper and he’s a very good boy.

verdict.reason: Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic vision with Josh Brolin and Margaret Qualley deserves a big screen and an audience. The early access and ensemble cast suggest Scott is taking a genuine creative swing, not chasing spectacle.

movies.title: Advance Screening: The Magic Faraway Tree

ratings.plot: Some kids tumble down rabbit holes. Others step through wardrobes. In THE MAGIC FARAWAY TREE, adventure begins with a climb on a swing. After moving to the English countryside, three siblings discover an enchanted tree whose highest branches lead to magical new worlds filled with unusual characters and unexpected detours. Starring Claire Foy and Andrew Garfield, this fantasy spins Enid Blyton's classic children’s book into an adventure where every trip up the tree drops the kids somewhere completely different. See it on the big screen for a healthy dose of whimsy.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you have young kids or nostalgia for Blyton—this adaptation lands somewhere between children's film and family spectacle, without the craft to justify either commitment. The cast and 110-minute runtime suggest studio ambition, but advance screenings of book adaptations rarely indicate the filmmakers found their voice.

ratings.plot: Ordinary word processor Paul Hackett experiences the worst night of his life after he agrees to visit Marcy, a Soho resident that he met that evening at a coffee shop.

verdict.reason: Scorsese's funniest film is a masterclass in escalating chaos and one of cinema's great fever dreams about the city turning hostile. The newly restored DCP at Metrograph sharpens the neon-soaked Manhattan nightmare that defined 1980s downtown cool.

ratings.plot: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents CATVIDEOFEST 2026, a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses. Each year, across the country, local theaters partner with nearby cat-focused charities, animal welfare associations, and shelters alike – a portion of ticket proceeds from every show goes directly to local cats in need.

verdict.reason: Seventy-five minutes of uncut cat content on a theater screen is the rare occasion when collective laughter beats solitary scrolling. Ticket proceeds go to local shelters, so you're funding rescue work while getting exactly what you came for.

ratings.plot: When three American doctors-Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian-enter Gaza to save lives, they find themselves caught between medicine and politics, risking everything to expose the truth.

verdict.reason: A urgent documentary about doctors navigating impossible choices in an active crisis—this is the kind of film that demands a theater and the moment it's playing. Poh Si Teng's debut has the immediacy and moral weight that justify leaving home tonight.

ratings.plot: Heroes from three different worlds must unite when they're thrust together to confront a catastrophic danger that could destroy everything they know.

verdict.reason: Skip it; Marvel's formula has run thin and 165 minutes of multiverse fan service doesn't justify a theatrical trip. The Russo Brothers are reliably competent but have nothing new to say about superhero spectacle.

ratings.plot: A group of professors working on a new encyclopedia while living in a Manhattan mansion take in a mouthy nightclub singer who is wanted by the police to help bring down her mob boss lover.

verdict.reason: Hawks' screwball masterpiece belongs on a theater screen, not your couch. Gary Cooper and Barbara Stanwyck generate enough electricity to power the whole city, and the rapid-fire dialogue demands full attention in a room full of people who'll laugh at the same moments you do.

ratings.plot: Our intrepid adolescent heroes wake up to find their beloved television stolen, and embark on an epic journey across America to recover it, and, who knows, maybe even score.

verdict.reason: A fun theatrical outing for the format's fans, but the theatrical cut is thin and the runtime is merciful only because it ends quickly. The Nitehawk screening offers communal laughs that a home viewing won't match, so go if you want to sit in a room full of people laughing at stupidity in real time.

ratings.plot: A young man and woman meet on a train in Europe, and wind up spending one evening together in Vienna. Unfortunately, both know that this will probably be their only night together.

verdict.reason: One of Linklater's essential films — a master class in dialogue and intimacy that demands the theater's full attention. Metrograph's restoration gives you the Vienna streets and faces in the clarity they deserve.

ratings.plot: Two young friends involved in organized crime and drug dealing find that their priorities differ.

verdict.reason: Hype Williams made a visual landmark in 1998 that still stands as one of the most stylistically assured debuts in American cinema. The Nitehawk screening is a rare chance to see this film's hallucinatory cinematography and production design on a proper theater screen where the visual density actually lands.

verdict.reason: This is a broad comedy that lands occasional laughs but doesn't justify a theater trip when it's freely available on streaming. The pairs skating setup is thin scaffolding for sketch-adjacent humor that plays better in a living room than in a packed IFC Center.

ratings.plot: A movie sound recordist accidentally records the evidence that proves that a car accident was actually murder and consequently finds himself in danger.

verdict.reason: De Palma's best thriller, a masterwork of paranoid cinema that demands the big screen for its elaborate setpieces and sound design. The climax alone—a meticulously constructed sequence at the Liberty Day parade—justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Bouchra, a 35-year-old Moroccan coyote in New York documents her long-distance relationship with her mother in Casablanca, as they explore together the love, pain and secrets that unite them through calls and intimate conversations.

verdict.reason: A tender animated film about mother and daughter separated by an ocean, made with real affection for its characters and their fractured intimacy. The hand-drawn work captures the texture of long-distance love in ways live-action cannot, and Metrograph's presentation honors the filmmakers' visual specificity.

ratings.plot: The life and death of "Dracula" writer Bram Stoker is discussed, as well as the themes of the novel and several film adaptations of "Dracula," and the cultural impact of the work. While critics of the time were not receptive to th...

verdict.reason: A compact documentary on Stoker's life and Dracula's cultural reach, worth an hour at Metrograph if you're curious about the novel's origins and film legacy. The DCP presentation is clean, but fifty-six minutes of talking heads and adaptation clips works just as well at home.

ratings.plot: Kristoffer is a billboard hanger, 24 years old and carefree. When his girlfriend Elisabeth dumps him for the boss of her trend bureau, his life falls into pieces. He feels like a loser. By coincidence some of Kristoffer's video di...

verdict.reason: Skip the subway unless you're tracking early Tyldum or need a breezy 100-minute palate cleanser. The film plays like a competent Norwegian rom-com from the early 2000s, best suited to a rainy afternoon at home rather than a theater seat tonight.

movies.title: Butthole Surfers: The Hole Truth and Nothing Butt

ratings.plot: A documentary feature about the legendary American punk band Butthole Surfers. The film tells the story of how two accounting students from Trinity College in San Antonio found solidarity in their weirdness, recruited like-minded misfits – queers, weirdos, and nonconformists like naked performance artist/dancer Kathleen Lynch – and embarked on one of the most radical rock journeys of all time. Somehow this band, with a defiantly non-commercial name, ended up as a major influence on acts like Nirvana and even scored a No. 1 hit song. Beyond the band’s story, the film tells the human story of the people behind the band. It gives an intimate look at lead singer Gibby Haynes, guitar wizard Paul Leary, drummers Teresa Nervosa and King Coffey, and bassist Jeff Pinkus – five American originals with incredible personal stories.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone who cares about American punk's weirdest and most influential act. The film captures five originals at the center of a genuinely radical career, told with the kind of intimate access that matters for a band built on refusal to compromise.

ratings.plot: Alice, an ambitious camgirl, wakes up one day to discover she's been replaced on her show with an exact replica of herself.

verdict.reason: A smart horror film about identity and digital labor that uses its premise to say something true about performance and violation. Goldhaber sustains the tension through tight 94 minutes and finds real dread in the uncanny—the double isn't a jump-scare trick but a slowly darkening mirror.

ratings.plot: Carrie White, a shy, friendless teenage girl who is sheltered by her domineering, religious mother, unleashes her telekinetic powers after being humiliated by her classmates at her senior prom.

verdict.reason: De Palma's horror masterpiece belongs on the big screen, where the split-screen prom sequence and Sissy Spacek's performance hit hardest. The Alamo locations will pack it with the right crowd.

ratings.plot: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses.

verdict.reason: Skip the trip unless you want 70 minutes of curated internet cat content on a theater screen with friends. The Alamo Drafthouse venues let you drink while watching, which is the only reason this works as a theatrical outing.

ratings.plot: Biopic of 1930s Chinese actress Lingyu Ruan.

verdict.reason: Stanley Kwan's 1991 masterpiece about Lingyu Ruan uses fragmented narrative and layered performance to interrogate cinema, stardom, and historical truth itself. Film Forum's repertory screening of this restored print is essential viewing for anyone serious about film history or the power of biographical cinema.

ratings.plot: Nina, a runaway bride, is unaware that her mother has married her fiancé in her stead, and that the two have set out to bring her back.

verdict.reason: The premise collapses under its own absurdity and the execution does not justify the runtime. A 94-minute film built on a single implausible plot twist has nowhere to go.

ratings.plot: In 2017, a successful businessman travels to the ends of the earth to find that the perfect woman is always under his nose. He hires a sexy renegade tracker to find an exact duplicate of his android wife.

verdict.reason: A dopey 80s sex-bot romp with genuine charm and a game cast, but the premise outstays its welcome well before the ninety-minute mark. The Alamo Drafthouse is the right venue for this kind of cult obscurity if you're in the mood for something deliberately silly.

ratings.plot: Single mother Vianne Rocher and her young daughter arrive in a rural French town in the winter of 1959, and open an unusual chocolate shop that disrupts the moral fiber of the strictly Catholic townsfolk and mayor.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you want a comfortable period drama with Depp and Firth that doesn't justify the runtime. The DCP at Metrograph is clean, but the film itself plays safer than the premise promises.

ratings.plot: An armchair mystery in which the life of a reclusive academic collides with the story of a clandestine technology that can photograph the past.

verdict.reason: An unreleased 2026 film with no director credited, no critical record, and no established reputation has no business taking up a theater seat tonight. Without any evidence of artistic merit or theatrical necessity, this is a placeholder, not a movie.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked romance is essential cinema on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation brings the saturated colors and kinetic editing to full life.

ratings.plot: An irresponsible, drug-addicted, recently impregnated woman finds herself in the middle of an abortion debate when both parties attempt to sway her to their respective sides.

verdict.reason: Payne's debut is a rare political comedy that punches in all directions without losing its humanity. The film's refusal to sanctify either side of its argument, combined with a genuinely committed performance from Laura Dern, makes it essential viewing in any era.

ratings.plot: Classical Period is a portrait of Cal and his friends in Philadelphia. They meet and have long conversations about books, poetry, music, and architecture, most notably Henry Longfellow's 1864 translation of Dante's Divine Comedy ....

verdict.reason: A 62-minute film of conversation about books and poetry has genuine charm, but it asks a lot of patience for modest rewards. Fendt's quiet naturalism works best on a smaller screen where you control the pacing.

ratings.plot: A cab driver finds himself the hostage of an engaging contract killer as he makes his rounds from hit to hit during one night in Los Angeles.

verdict.reason: Mann's night-vision Los Angeles is a character unto itself, and the cat-and-mouse dialogue between Cruise and Foxx justifies the theatrical investment. Tom Cruise's silver-haired killer is one of cinema's most magnetic villains, and Mann shoots the city with the precision of a heist film.

ratings.plot: A reclusive retired professor is faced with confronting modernity when a group of vulgar youths led by an obnoxious marchesa take up residence in his unused upper residence.

verdict.reason: Visconti's final film is a sharp class collision that rewards the runtime with its glacial, merciless pacing. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings the palette of this Fascist-era meditation into sharp focus.

ratings.plot: It's Girl Scout Cookie season, and four tenacious girls strive to be a top-selling "Cookie Queen," navigating an $800 million business in which innocence and ambition collide.
A criminal psychologist who turned agoraphobic after a murder attempt agrees to help two San Francisco detectives hunt for a copycat serial killer who intends on making her his next victim.

verdict.reason: A sharp 90s thriller with real tension between Sigourney Weaver's agoraphobic psychologist and the serial killer hunting her, but the runtime drags and the third act relies on plot mechanics rather than character. The theatrical experience matters here—Weaver's claustrophobia plays better on a big screen than at home.

verdict.reason: A three-hour opera film demands commitment, but Metge's take on Mozart's comedy has real wit if you're in the mood for theatrical excess. The Lincoln Center screening gives you the proper scale, though streaming at home won't punish you much.

ratings.plot: A story set in the ACME warehouse, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a theatrical release of a film that was shelved for years, suggesting the studio itself lost faith in the project. Dave Green's direction of a live-action/CGI hybrid based on a thin premise about an ACME warehouse does not justify the subway ride when better animated comedies are streaming.

ratings.plot: American professor John Holden arrives in London for a parapsychology conference, only to find himself investigating the mysterious actions of Devil-worshipper Julian Karswell.

verdict.reason: Tourneur's 1957 masterpiece of atmospheric dread belongs on the big screen where its shadow-work and mounting tension hit hardest. The restoration at Lincoln Center is the place to experience this film's command of mood and its rare balance of supernatural terror and intellectual rigor.

ratings.plot: Through 10 years of family archives, we follow the life of Liena, an immigrant mother who faces the challenge of raising her two children in Spain, one of whom is autistic.

verdict.reason: A decade of family footage documenting an immigrant mother raising two children in Spain has emotional weight, but the film's power depends entirely on your tolerance for intimate, unstructured domestic cinema. Anthology's DCP projection honors the archival material, though the experience works just as well on a smaller screen.

movies.title: Days and Nights in the Forest

verdict.reason: Essential Ray on the big screen — this ranks among his finest character studies. The Metrograph restoration reveals the subtle interplay between natural light and psychological insight that makes his camera work irreplaceable.

ratings.plot: A documentary about writer and director Brian De Palma.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone serious about cinema craft and narrative design. Baumbach and Paltrow let De Palma himself do the teaching, breaking down how he builds suspense and composes a frame with the precision of a surgeon.

ratings.plot: Mercenaries with nothing to lose are hired to rescue a bioengineer imprisoned in a cold war bunker. Upon entering the ominous facility, they find themselves in a fight for their lives when they come under attack from an unknown an...

verdict.reason: Skip it; the premise of mercenaries versus lab horrors in a bunker has been executed better elsewhere and this 91-minute film doesn't justify a trip to Williamsburg. The action-horror hybrid needs either sharp direction or a novel angle, and Matthew Ninaber's execution here lands in the disposable middle.

ratings.plot: Intent on seeing the Cahulawassee River before it's dammed and turned into a lake, outdoor fanatic Lewis Medlock takes his friends on a canoeing trip they'll never forget into the dangerous American back-country.

verdict.reason: One of the great survival films—see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where Boorman's control of landscape and danger plays at full force. The river itself becomes the antagonist, and the print restores details in light and shadow that streaming flattens.

ratings.plot: When a southern Italian town is rocked by a string of child murders, the police and two urban outcasts search for the culprit amid scapegoating within the superstitious community.

ratings.plot: Green Beret veteran Rambo takes on a Pacific Northwest sheriff and the National Guard.

verdict.reason: A Rohmer film about friendship and class collision belongs on the big screen, and this Metrograph restoration captures the precise social observation that makes his work essential. ratings.plot: In a French seaside town, at a boarding house for civil servants recovering from surgery and maladies, the six male residents' lives change dramatically when two women arrive: Catherine, lively, sexually liberated, willing to kiss...

verdict.reason: Skip it; the 1995 anime original is the essential version and remains superior on every technical level. This live-action remake adds nothing except hollow spectacle and arrives a quarter-century too late.

ratings.plot: Captured live over the course of GHOST’s two sold-out shows in Mexico City last year, 2 BIG TO RIG is the definitive document of the band's unforgettable SKELETOUR WORLD TOUR. Shot on 16mm film, GHOST has never looked or sounded better, ripping through material from the band's six albums, including 2025’s global #1 Skeletá as well as non-LP favorites including “Mary On A Cross,” “Kiss the Go-Goat,” and “The Future is a Foreign Land.”

verdict.reason: Skip the trip unless you're committed to the band; this is a live document for the faithful, not a gateway. The 16mm cinematography and phone-free setlist footage have real texture, but you're paying theatrical prices for what amounts to a premium bootleg.

ratings.plot: A girl with few real prospects joins a gang, reinventing herself and gaining a sense of self confidence in the process. However, she soon finds that this new life does not necessarily make her any happier.

verdict.reason: Sciamma captures the texture of female adolescence with visual precision and restraint that most coming-of-age films never achieve. The 4:3 aspect ratio and handheld intimacy at Metrograph demand the theatrical frame.

ratings.plot: Two boys begin a silence strike to press their parents into buying them a television set.

ratings.plot: After a botched bank robbery lands his younger brother in prison, Connie Nikas embarks on a twisted odyssey through New York City's underworld to get his brother Nick out of jail.

ratings.plot: On a dark, wet night a historic and regal Chinese cinema sees its final film. Together with a small handful of souls they bid "Goodbye, Dragon Inn".

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's elegiac final night in a movie palace is essential viewing on a theater's big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph honors both the filmmaker's precision and the cinema it mourns.

movies.title: Grateful Dead Meet-Up at the Movies 2026

ratings.plot: Come celebrate the 35th anniversary of an iconic Grateful Dead show as it makes a high-energy return to the big screen! This can't-miss event features the complete June 17, 1991, concert from Giants Stadium. The performance launches with a shocking "Eyes Of The World," finding the band in peak form from the very first notes. The setlist continues, seamlessly blending beloved classics like "Truckin'" and "Uncle John's Band" with rarities such as "Saint of Circumstance," "Might As Well," "New Speedway Boogie," and "China Doll." The major highlight of the night is the continuous teases of "Dark Star" edging its way in and out through the evening at six different points before finally exploding into the full song. The Dead capped off the spectacular night with The Band's "The Weight," a perfect song to send the crowd on its way. Considered one of the greatest shows of the band's final decade of performing, 6/17/91 offers a unique auditory experience as one of only two shows captured on 48-track tape. Enjoy a masterful surround sound mix by Jeffrey Norman and multi-camera visuals, featuring a rare cinematic appearance by both Bruce Hornsby and Vince Welnick. As a bonus, this extraordinary screening will also feature an exclusive sneak preview of the legendary "Shakedown Street" from the upcoming Merriweather 6/30/85 release, and a special introduction by Grateful Dead legacy manager and audio archivist David Lemieux. Join us, won't you?

verdict.reason: Skip the bootleg; this is the definitive capture of 6/17/91 in full surround sound and multi-camera on a big screen. The six-point "Dark Star" weave alone justifies the trip, and you'll be sitting in a room full of people who actually care.

ratings.plot: Lonely residents of a tornado-stricken Ohio town wander the deserted landscape trying to fulfill their boring, nihilistic lives.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're committed to Harmony Korine's aesthetic provocation and can handle 89 minutes of deliberate ugliness as cinema. The film prioritizes shock and style over narrative or emotional stakes, making it a harder watch than a rewarding one.

ratings.plot: A musical juxtaposition of the Orpheus/Eurydice and Hades/Persephone myths that examines the way real life can impact our quest for a perfect world.

verdict.reason: This is a rare theatrical capture of one of the great stage musicals of the past decade. Anaïs Mitchell's songs and Rachel Chavkin's direction demand the big screen and theater sound.

ratings.plot: Living in exile, Dr. Hannibal Lecter tries to reconnect with now disgraced F.B.I. Agent Clarice Starling, and finds himself a target of revenge from a powerful victim.

verdict.reason: Ridley Scott's baroque excess and 35mm presentation at Metrograph salvage a sequel that collapses under its own ambition. The runtime bloats a thin premise, but the visual design and Scott's commitment to style over substance reward patient viewers on the big screen.

ratings.plot: A slow-burning epic chronicling the emotional journey of four thirty something women in the misty seaside city of Kobe.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip if you can commit to three hours of Hamaguchi's patient, attentive filmmaking about friendship and time. Metrograph's screening rewards the runtime with a proper theatrical space for a film that earns every minute of its duration.

ratings.plot: A couple take a trip to Argentina but both men find their lives drifting apart in opposite directions.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at his visual peak—worth the trip for a masterwork of color, movement, and heartbreak on the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph lets you see every saturated frame and tracking shot as intended.

ratings.plot: Two killers stop at Olga's gas station alongside a California highway.

verdict.reason: A lean 1934 crime picture with genuine tension, but its 63 minutes feel padded and the theatrical experience at Nitehawk doesn't compensate for a film better suited to home viewing. Mervyn LeRoy directs with competence, not invention, and the gas station setting, while clever, never quite ignites.

ratings.plot: Arriving in Chicago, Henry moves in with ex-con acquaintance Otis and starts schooling him in the ways of the serial killer.

verdict.reason: This is essential viewing on a big screen—a landmark film about violence that refuses to aestheticize or exploit what it shows. McNaughton's deadpan direction and grainy 16mm stock make the brutality feel documentary-real in a way that home viewing completely loses.

Skip the new horror remakes and catch Nobuhiko Obayashi's 1977 masterpiece instead. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, the only way to experience this hallucinogenic, formally wild film about a haunted house that operates on pure visual logic and dream logic rather than plot.

movies.title: How to Divorce During the War

ratings.plot: Set in Vilnius in 2022, high-flying executive Marija chooses the worst moment to discuss divorce with husband Vytas - one day before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The couple navigates separation amid a refugee crisis.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds emotional clarity in catastrophic timing, using a single marriage to frame the chaos of invasion. Blazevicius shoots Vilnius with the precision of a architect documenting a city about to break.

ratings.plot: A group of shoplifters take aim at a cutthroat fashion maven by stealing her clothes and reselling them at a lower price, what they call "fashion-forward philanthropy."

ratings.plot: An idyllic summer town descends into madness when an ice cream man serves kids sweet delights with horrifying results.

verdict.reason: Skip it; Eli Roth's premise—horror built on poisoned ice cream—is thin enough for a short film, not a feature that needs 106 minutes to justify itself. The execution here doesn't earn the runtime or a theater ticket when streaming will deliver the same half-baked idea without the subway fare.

ratings.plot: A woman grows increasingly fascinated with her body after suffering a disfiguring accident.

verdict.reason: Marina de Van's debut is a fearless work of body horror that deserves the theatrical intensity of Metrograph's screen. The DCP presentation honors the film's unflinching close-ups and the precise craft of a filmmaker working through transgression and self-destruction.

ratings.plot: Two neighbors form a strong bond after both suspect extramarital activities of their spouses. However, they agree to keep their bond platonic so as not to commit similar wrongs.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's masterpiece deserves the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the chromatic precision that defines his visual language. The film's emotional restraint and compositional density reveal themselves only in a theater.

ratings.plot: In 1938, after his father goes missing while pursuing the Holy Grail, Indiana Jones finds himself up against the Nazis again to stop them from obtaining its powers.

verdict.reason: Spielberg at his most assured—a perfect blend of action, humor, and genuine emotional weight that justifies a theatrical revisit. The father-son dynamic and Sean Connery's performance elevate this above standard adventure fare.

ratings.plot: Gemma, a young mother raising her daughter in the house she grew up in, discovers she can travel into The Further, where she possesses an ability to bring what lives there back to the real world.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the franchise has exhausted its premise, and a sixth entry banking on hereditary horror and dimension-hopping adds nothing new. Jacob Chase's direction has not yet earned the benefit of the doubt on material this thin.

ratings.plot: Events over the course of one traumatic night in Paris unfold in reverse-chronological order.

verdict.reason: Only worth the trip if you can handle Noé's most punishing work without walking out. The reverse chronology structure and 13-minute single-take rape scene make this an endurance test that demands big-screen commitment.

ratings.plot: A newly-possessed high-school cheerleader turns into a succubus who specializes in killing her male classmates. Can her best friend put an end to the horror?

verdict.reason: Kusama's genre instincts have only sharpened since 2009, and this film's blend of teenage friendship and body horror feels prescient now. Metrograph's DCP restoration gives the neon-soaked cinematography the theatrical clarity it deserves.

ratings.plot: New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison discovers there's more to the Kennedy assassination than the official story.

ratings.plot: What happens when you get Sandra Bullock, Nicole Kidman, Stockard Channing, and Dianne Wiest together? You get one of the most magical witch movies of the '90s next to HOCUS POCUS! ratings.plot: After a drug-fueled car crash, ex-private schoolboys Ayden and Jesse escape into the Melbourne CBD and are plunged into a night of unbridled debauchery and rapidly escalating violence.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the film squanders a solid premise with sloppy execution and self-indulgent direction that mistakes chaos for consequence. At 93 minutes it still feels bloated, and Aroni's style prioritizes surface-level provocation over any genuine insight into his characters or their spiral.

ratings.plot: The oncologist wife of a prominent child psychologist suspects her husband has an unhealthy scientific obsession with their child, unaware of what - or who - is really going on inside his head.

verdict.reason: De Palma's split-screen machinations and fractured narrative deserve the big screen, but the film's schematic plotting undercuts its psychological reach. The Alamo's print is clean, though this is a film that rewards patience more than surprise.

ratings.plot: A young woman, studying to be a vet, develops a craving for human flesh.

verdict.reason: Ducournau's debut is a rare horror film that earns its extremity through formal precision and genuine artistic vision. Metrograph's DCP presentation showcases the film's composed cinematography and color work, which are essential to how the body horror lands.

ratings.plot: A self-conscious woman juggles adjusting to her new role as an aristocrat's wife and avoiding being intimidated by his first wife's spectral presence.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's only Best Picture winner holds up as a masterclass in psychological suspense and Gothic atmosphere on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the shadows and compositions that make this 1940 film feel as immediate as a modern thriller.

ratings.plot: The parallel coming-of-age stories of a father living in Sarajevo during World War II and his son living through the Siege of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War.

verdict.reason: A rare Bosnian film about generational trauma across two wars deserves to be seen on a big screen. Film Forum's programming of this restoration makes it a necessary theatrical moment for a film that has circulated too little outside festival circuits.

ratings.plot: Documentary filmmaker Ross McElwee sets out to make a movie about Union General Sherman's March to the Sea towards the end of the American Civil War, but keeps getting sidetracked by his own love life.

ratings.plot: A grieving father enacts his long-awaited revenge against a ruthless gang on Christmas Eve.

verdict.reason: John Woo's first English-language film in years has genuine craft moments, but the execution is uneven and the premise wears thin before the final act. The Lincoln Center booking is respectable, but this is a minor entry from a major director—worth catching only if you're committed to tracking his recent work.

ratings.plot: Tells the story of the six wives of Henry VIII, reimagining them as pop stars who reclaim their narratives from their infamous husband's shadow.

verdict.reason: The stage production has genuine energy and the live concert format gives it theatrical urgency, but the 95-minute runtime and familiar material make this a better fit for devoted fans than casual theatergoers. The Alamo Drafthouse venues offer a more relaxed viewing experience than a traditional movie theater, which suits the event nature of the broadcast.

movies.title: Six: The Musical Live! Early Screening

ratings.plot: Winner of over 35 awards, experience the best of British musical HER-story in a live capture of the must-see musical sensation, SIX the Musical . verdict.reason: A filmed stage performance works best if you cannot see the real thing, but this West End capture on a theater screen lacks the liveness that makes musicals breathe in person. The 98-minute runtime respects your night better than a full stage show, yet you are watching actors perform for cameras in a playhouse, not for you in a cinema.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're in the mood for a comedy that swings wildly between sincere and absurd, which makes it uneven but occasionally inspired. Dylan Meyer's debut feature leans on character chemistry to carry the telepathy premise, and that works better in a theater than it will streaming, but the script undercuts itself too often to make the trip essential.

movies.title: The Wrong Girls Best Buds Screening

ratings.plot: It's been a while since we got a good old-fashioned stoner comedy on the big screen. Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat star as codependent best friends scraping by paycheck to paycheck and bong rip to bong rip until a case of mistaken identity sends them into increasingly absurd trouble. Produced by the team behind BLOCKERS, THE WRONG GIRLS also features Seth Rogen and Kumail Nanjiani as the voices of two talking cats, which feels exactly right.

verdict.reason: A lightweight stoner comedy with charm in its cast chemistry, but 100 minutes of mistaken-identity hijinks wears thin fast. The talking cats bit suggests the film knows how to lean into absurdity, which saves it from total disposability—catch it at Alamo Drafthouse if you want low-stakes fun and the social experience of the venue.

movies.title: There Once Was a Singing Blackbird

ratings.plot: A carefree young percussionist roams the streets of Tbilisi, interacting with friends and strangers alike, and tries to avoid responsibilities.

verdict.reason: A rare chance to see Iosseliani's debut in a restored DCP at Metrograph. The film's gentle comedy and kinetic street-level observation of Tbilisi justify the trip for anyone interested in Soviet-era cinema outside the monumental tradition.

ratings.plot: While doing a thesis about violence, Ángela finds a snuff video where a girl is tortured until death. Soon she discovers that the girl was a former student in her faculty...

verdict.reason: Amenábar's debut is a taut thriller that earns its intellectual premise through genuine suspense and formal craft. The film builds dread through meticulous editing and sound design rather than cheap shocks, making this 1996 Spanish landmark worth seeing on a big screen at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: After years in prison, ace safe-cracker Frank owns a car dealership and a cocktail lounge, which are fronts for high-stakes jewelry heists. He wants to complete one last big heist for the Mob before he goes straight.

verdict.reason: Mann's neon-soaked masterpiece about obsession and control demands the big screen and theatrical sound. James Caan's performance is ice-cold perfection, and the heist sequences are shot with such visual precision they feel like pure cinema.

ratings.plot: A group of troubled teenagers are led by social workers on a California wilderness retreat, not knowing that the woods they are camping in have become infested by mutated, blood-sucking ticks.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the premise of mutant ticks attacking teens in the woods has aged into generic creature-feature territory with no theatrical urgency. At 85 minutes, it's short enough to stream on a slow night if the concept appeals to you.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Matt Johnson finds the formative moment in Bourdain's life—a summer kitchen apprenticeship that teaches hunger and ambition before fame—and makes it feel urgent and alive. The specificity of place and time, grounded in Johnson's eye for how character emerges from work and friction, gives this a theatrical weight that matters.

ratings.plot: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the rest of the gang's jobs are challenged when they're introduced to electronics, a new threat to playtime.

verdict.reason: Pixar's best franchise entry in over a decade finds real weight in obsolescence and what toys mean when play itself is dying. Stanton's direction moves the camera with purpose, and the script trusts the audience to sit with melancholy before the inevitable uplift.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A restrained zombie film that uses genre mechanics to examine human selfishness under pressure—rare enough to justify the trip. The restoration at IFC Center sharpens the kinetic train-set staging that made this work in the first place.

ratings.plot: In Detroit, a pop-culture enthusiast steals cocaine from his new wife's pimp and tries to sell it in Hollywood, prompting the mobsters who own the drugs to pursue the couple.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's greatest film—a pulp romance that moves with genuine velocity and heartbreak. The Metrograph screening gives you the color saturation and kinetic editing that define Scott's visual language.

ratings.plot: Two storm chasers on the brink of divorce must work together to create an advanced weather alert system by putting themselves in the cross-hairs of extremely violent tornadoes.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a dated blockbuster that plays better on home video where you control the pacing. Jan de Bont's direction prioritizes spectacle over character, and the 113 minutes of chasing feels repetitive on a big screen without the novelty that made it work in 1996.

ratings.plot: A young woman struggles with completing a ritual centered around a menacing fertility plant in order to ensure that her bloodline continues.

verdict.reason: A short horror film about botanical body horror has limited theatrical draw and works better as part of a curated program than as a solo ticket. The premise trades on familiar occult-fertility tropes without the runtime or scope to justify a dedicated theater visit.

ratings.plot: A former San Francisco police detective juggles wrestling with his personal demons and becoming obsessed with the hauntingly beautiful woman he has been hired to trail, who may be deeply disturbed.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's greatest achievements belongs on the big screen, and this 35mm print at Metrograph is the way to experience Hitchcock's command of color, space, and visual obsession. The vertigo effect and San Francisco locations demand theatrical scale to hit their full hypnotic power.

ratings.plot: After a bad gambling bet, a schoolteacher is marooned in a town full of crazy, drunk, violent men who threaten to make him just as crazy, drunk, and violent.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about masculine violence and social collapse—see it on the big screen while you can. Metrograph is showing a restored DCP of a 1971 masterpiece that demands theater sound and image to land its full nightmare force.

ratings.plot: Two city-bred siblings are stranded in the Australian Outback, where they learn to survive with the aid of an Aboriginal boy on his "walkabout": a ritual separation from his tribe.

verdict.reason: Roeg's visual command of the Outback is unmatched on small screens, and this 35mm print at Metrograph restores the color and light that define the film's language. The cinematography is the story.

ratings.plot: What seems to be the ideal setting for fun and relaxation quickly turns deadly when six vacationing college students encounter a cursed spirit with an insatiable appetite.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a forgettable slasher with no distinctive voice or visual style. The creature design and kills lack the ingenuity needed to justify a theatrical trip over streaming at home.

ratings.plot: Set on the last day of camp, in the hot summer of 1981, a group of counselors try to complete their unfinished business before the day ends.

verdict.reason: This comedy has become a cult classic that rewards repeat viewing and plays brilliantly in a theater full of people who get the joke. David Wain's absurdist energy and the ensemble's commitment to deadpan nonsense make this a rare case where initial critical dismissal undersells what actually lands on screen.

movies.title: Wet Hot American Summer: 25th Anniversary Party

ratings.plot: Remember those kids who were too cool for school? Those kids are now your camp counselors. David Wain and company (including members of MTV's The State , the Upright Citizens Brigade, SNL , and a pre-famed Bradley Cooper) make idiosyncratic, over-the-top. strangely touching comedy. These character creations are unlike anything you've ever seen AND people you can relate to. There's young love, steamy sessions in the shed, talking cans, and everybody's favorite activity...going to town! So relive this unbelievably watchable, funny, original movie. It doesn't give one single f*ck...and that's the best part.

verdict.reason: Skip a special screening unless you have nostalgia for the original or want to catch the ensemble cast in a room together. The theatrical experience doesn't add much that the home version doesn't deliver, and the film plays better when you can pause it.

ratings.plot: The wife of a university research scientist believes that her lakeside Vermont home is haunted by a ghost - or that she is losing her mind.

verdict.reason: Zemeckis's craft elevates a thin supernatural mystery into something watchable, but the 130-minute runtime drags a third-act twist that doesn't earn its setup. The 35mm print at Metrograph is the only reason to see it in a theater instead of streaming.

ratings.plot: Anna, a shy 12-year-old girl, is sent to spend time with her aunt and uncle who live in the countryside, where she meets Marnie. The two become best friends. But Anna gradually discovers that Marnie is not quite who she appears to...

verdict.reason: Studio Ghibli's final feature is a delicate ghost story about loneliness and connection that demands the big screen. Yonebayashi's watercolor animation and the Metrograph's DCP projection bring out textures that would dissolve on a small display.

ratings.plot: Eight-year-old Ahmed has mistakenly taken his friend Mohammad's notebook. He wants to return it, or else his friend will be expelled from school. The boy determinedly sets out to find Mohammad's home in the neighbouring village.

verdict.reason: Kiarostami's breakthrough transforms a simple premise into profound cinema. The Iranian landscape and natural light create images that lose impact on small screens.

ratings.plot: A humble clerk courts a woman who awaits her lover's return night after night.

verdict.reason: Visconti's 1957 masterwork on desire and self-deception belongs on the big screen, and Film Forum's restoration makes this the time to see it. The nocturnal Rome cinematography and Marcello Mastroianni's performance justify the trip.

ratings.plot: Two sloppy actors spend a weekend holiday at an uncle's country cottage.

verdict.reason: One of the funniest British comedies ever made—see it on the big screen where every line lands harder. Metrograph's DCP restoration sharpens the deadpan timing and gives the bleakness of 1980s London the visual weight it deserves.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar at peak invention, vital in 35mm. The 88-minute runtime moves like a perfectly wound toy, and Metrograph's print restores the saturated color palette that makes every frame feel like a poster.

ratings.plot: A bullied girl transfers schools hoping for peace, but her past trauma isolates her-until she discovers a series of secret letters hidden around the school, leading her on a mysterious quest to uncover their sender's true intent.

verdict.reason: A competent animated drama about isolation and connection, but the mystery-box structure relies on emotional payoff that may not justify the runtime on a big screen. Kim Yong-Hwan's direction is serviceable rather than visually urgent, making this better suited to home viewing unless you need a gentler theatrical option tonight.
